passage:
The rain had knocked out the streetlights, so Sahil and Ganga stood under the bus-stop roof in the dark, waiting for a bus already twenty minutes late.
"Can I say something that's been bothering me?" Ganga said. "I've been trying to find the right way for a week." She took a breath. "At the studio, you keep interrupting the junior designers. They've stopped speaking in meetings. I don't think you see it."
Sahil's face went hot. He wanted to say she was exaggerating. But he noticed her hands twisting the strap of her bag, and how carefully she had chosen each word.
The bus finally splashed up. On the ride he replayed Tuesday's meeting and the junior who had started a sentence and stopped. "Thanks," he texted her that night. "That can't have been easy to say."

qa.a: She said he keeps interrupting the junior designers.

qa.q: What did Sahil feel at first, and what changed his reaction?
qa.a: He felt stung and defensive, his face hot, but noticing her twisting hands and careful words showed him she cared, so he listened.

qa.q: What did Sahil do that shows he took the feedback well?
qa.a: He replayed Tuesday's meeting, remembered the junior who stopped mid-sentence, and texted Ganga to thank her.

qa.q: What was it like for Ganga to say it?
qa.a: It was hard for her; she had searched for the right way for a week and twisted her bag strap while speaking.

passage:
On their evening walk round the colony park in Hyderabad, Shalini slowed down near the swings. "Pradeep, I'm only saying this because I've known you since school." He laughed. "Uh oh."
"You've borrowed from three of us this year and paid everyone back late. Nobody says anything. But they've stopped inviting you to plan trips, and I think that's why."
Pradeep stopped walking. His ears burned. He wanted to list every reason: the rent, his mother's bills. Instead he stared at the swings. She hadn't said it in the group or by text. She had waited for a quiet walk and said it looking at him.
"That stings," he said finally.
"I know. I'd rather it stung from me."
Two days later he messaged her a list of what he owed, with dates. "Hold me to it?"

qa.q: How many people had Pradeep borrowed from this year?
qa.a: He had borrowed from three of them this year.

qa.q: How did Pradeep feel when Shalini spoke, and what shows it?
qa.a: He felt stung and embarrassed; his ears burned and he wanted to list excuses, but he stared at the swings instead.

qa.q: What choice did Pradeep make two days later, and why was it wise?
qa.a: He sent Shalini a list of what he owed, with dates, and asked her to hold him to it, turning the hard truth into a plan.

qa.q: Why might Shalini have chosen a quiet walk to say it?
qa.a: She cared about him and wanted to spare him public embarrassment, preferring the sting to come privately from someone who had known him since school.

grounding: An adult hears a hard truth about his borrowing habit from an old school companion, feels stung, then acts on it, seeing the care in how gently she said it.

passage:
I'm Ritu, and last winter my friend Anand told me something I didn't want to hear.
We'd been friends since college. One evening he asked if we could walk by the lake instead of meeting at the café. Halfway round, he stopped. "Ritu, can I tell you something difficult? I've been nervous about it for weeks."
I laughed. "Go on."
"In team meetings, you interrupt people. Especially the juniors. I've watched Nisha stop talking three times this month. I don't think you notice."
My face went hot. I wanted to say he was exaggerating. I said, "Wow. Okay," and walked faster.
That night I couldn't sleep. I replayed the last meeting. He was right.
What stays with me is that he walked me all the way round the lake to say it. He'd clearly planned the words so they wouldn't cut. People who don't care just complain behind your back.

qa.q: Where did Anand ask to walk instead of the café?
qa.a: By the lake.

qa.q: How did Ritu feel when Anand first said it?
qa.a: Ritu felt stung and defensive, her face going hot, wanting to say he was exaggerating.

qa.q: What could Ritu do in the next team meeting?
qa.a: Ritu could consciously wait until juniors like Nisha finish speaking, and maybe thank Anand for his honesty.

qa.q: What does Anand's walk around the lake suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests Anand felt nervous but cared a lot, planning gentle words because the friendship mattered to him.

grounding: It shows an adult first stung and then grateful after a caring friend gently tells a hard truth about interrupting others.

passage:
Ward supervisor's note, night shift, Tuesday.
At handover this morning, Rashmi, our senior nurse, asked Afreen to stay back for five minutes. I was at the desk and saw most of it.
Rashmi said quietly, "Your patients love you. I hear it every shift. But your charting has gaps. Twice this week, the next shift didn't know a dose had been given. I'm telling you because I think you'll be a brilliant nurse, and this could hurt you."
Afreen's jaw tightened. She said, "Everyone's rushed at night," and looked away.
Rashmi didn't argue. She just said, "I know. Let me show you the shortcut I use."
An hour later, I saw Afreen go back to the station and thank her. She said, "I was angry for about ten minutes. Then I realised you stayed after a twelve-hour shift to tell me."
I've asked Rashmi to run a short charting session for all the juniors.

qa.q: How many times this week did the next shift not know a dose had been given?
qa.a: Twice this week.

qa.q: How did Afreen feel when Rashmi first raised the charting gaps?
qa.a: Afreen felt stung and defensive, her jaw tightening, and she made an excuse about everyone being rushed.

qa.q: What made Rashmi's feedback easier to accept?
qa.a: She spoke privately, started with real praise, explained why it mattered, and offered to show her shortcut.

qa.q: How does Rashmi seem to see Afreen?
qa.a: Rashmi sees Afreen as a future brilliant nurse, which is why she cared enough to stay after a long shift to tell her.

grounding: A supervisor records an adult stung and then grateful after a caring senior tells her a hard truth about her work gently.

subtype: Receiving hard truth from someone who cares [Receiver]
passage:
Saturday night
Nitin said it today. We were at the bus stop after the match, and he said, "Pranav, can I say something without you getting angry? You've cancelled on us nine times since March. Always the last minute. Everyone stopped counting on you."
I got angry anyway. I said, "So you've been keeping score?" and got on my bus without saying bye.
The whole ride home I was furious. Then less furious. Then I counted. Birthdays, the trek, Nitin's housewarming, my own plan for the movie. It was more than nine.
And what gets me is how he said it. He had clearly thought about it. He waited till we were alone. He said "us" and not "everyone thinks you're useless."
I just messaged him: "You're right. Sorry about the bus. Thanks for telling me." He replied with a thumbs up and "Sunday cricket? You in?"
I'm in. I'm actually going.

qa.q: How many times had Pranav cancelled since March, according to Nitin?
qa.a: He said Pranav had cancelled on them nine times since March.

qa.q: How did Pranav's feelings change on the ride home?
qa.a: Pranav went from angry and defensive to less furious, and finally grateful once he counted the cancellations himself.

qa.q: What did Pranav do once he realised Nitin was right?
qa.a: Pranav messaged Nitin to admit it, apologise for the bus, thank him, and say yes to Sunday cricket.

qa.q: How can you tell Nitin cared about Pranav when he spoke?
qa.a: Nitin had planned his words, waited until they were alone, and said "us," showing he wanted to help rather than hurt.

grounding: A diary shows an adult first angry and then grateful after a caring friend gently tells a hard truth about constant cancelling.
